claims.text: Simulation-optimized processing can drive a large-scale reaction between RHEA constituents and Cu despite their positive mixing enthalpy.
The proposed processing will produce a stable, well-bonded RHEA-Cu composite microstructure.
The starting material is a powder blend or premixed feedstock containing RHEA constituents and Cu particles.
Spark plasma sintering or laser powder bed fusion can provide the rapid thermal processing needed for the proposed RHEA-Cu reaction.
A DFT-informed machine-learning potential can be used to determine transient heating rates and dwell times at a Cu/refractory interface.
Controlled rapid heating and cooling under high-temperature conditions suppresses undesirable phase segregation.
Controlled reactive mixing at the RHEA-Cu interface reduces segregation.
Controlled interfacial mixing promotes a coherent and stabilized RHEA-Cu composite structure.
High-rate thermal processing generates localized melting followed by rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching kinetically suppresses segregation driven by the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
Simulation-guided parameters permit precise control of reaction kinetics and interfacial evolution.
Control of reaction kinetics and interface evolution enables a large-scale, uniform bond between Cu and the refractory matrix.
The processed composite will have greater interfacial bonding and homogeneity and less phase separation.
The processed RHEA-Cu composite will retain mechanical strength appropriate for nuclear-reactor applications.
The processed RHEA-Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance appropriate for nuclear-reactor applications.
Conventional sintering or casting of RHEA-Cu materials typically produces substantial phase segregation and unstable microstructures because of positive mixing enthalpy.
The method succeeds only within a specific simulation-derived processing window.
Heating rates or dwell times outside the processing window may cause phase segregation, inadequate reaction control, or loss of functional properties.
The numerical optimum for heating rates and dwell times has not yet been determined.
Industrial-scale applicability of the proposed parameter window remains unvalidated.
